title: Maximum OR
statement:
You get an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`. A single move picks any element of `nums` and doubles it in place. You may make up to `k` moves in total, and the same element may be picked again and again.

After your moves, take the bitwise OR of every element of `nums`. Return the biggest such OR you can reach. The result can exceed 32 bits, so it is a 64-bit integer.
notes:
## Intuition

Doubling a number shifts its bits one place left. Whichever element ends up holding the highest set bit decides the top of the result, and pushing that bit higher is worth more than anything the lower bits can add. So it never pays to split the moves: all `k` doublings go to one element, which becomes `nums[i] << k`. A brute force would try every way to spread the moves, but we only need to try each `i` as the single target.

For a fixed `i`, the result is `(nums[i] << k)` ORed with every other element unchanged. Prefix and suffix ORs give "every other element" in O(1).

## Approach

1. Build `suffix`, where `suffix[i]` is the OR of `nums[i..n-1]` and `suffix[n] = 0`.
2. Walk `i` from left to right, keeping `prefix` as the OR of `nums[0..i-1]`.
3. `others = prefix | suffix[i + 1]` is the OR of everything except `nums[i]`.
4. Shift `nums[i]` left by `k` as a BigInt, OR it with `others`, and keep the largest `value` in `best`.
5. Fold `nums[i]` into `prefix` and continue. Return `best` as a number.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [12, 9]`, `k = 1`. `suffix = [13, 9, 0]`.

- `i = 0`: `others = 0 | 9 = 9`, `value = 24 | 9 = 25`. `best = 25`, `prefix = 12`.
- `i = 1`: `others = 12 | 0 = 12`, `value = 18 | 12 = 30`. `best = 30`.

The answer is `30`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass builds `suffix`, one pass tries every element.
- Space: O(n) for the `suffix` array.

## Pitfalls

- JavaScript's `|` and `<<` work on 32-bit integers, but `nums[i] << k` can reach about 3.3 · 10^13. Do the shift and the final OR with BigInt (or a 64-bit `long` in Java and C).
- `prefix` and `suffix` stay below 2^30 because every `nums[i]` does, so plain numbers are safe for them.
- Doubling the largest element is not always best: for `[6, 5]` with `k = 1`, doubling 5 gives `10 | 6 = 14`, while doubling 6 gives only `12 | 5 = 13`. Try every index.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `suffix[i]` | OR of `nums[i]` through the end |
| `prefix` | OR of the elements before `i` |
| `shift` | `k` as a BigInt shift amount |
| `others` | OR of every element except `nums[i]` |
| `value` | the total OR when all moves go to `nums[i]` |
| `best` | the largest `value` so far |
